newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin op nears, Moscow power fight flares.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin op nears, Moscow power fight flares.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's heart operation may take place next week, according to his top foreign medical consultant.
But as the 65-year-old president prepared in Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow for surgery intended to see him through his four-year term, a fresh political row flared in the Kremlin.

Pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, who is expected to advise the Russian doctors who would carry out bypass surgery to improve blood circulation in Yeltsin's heart, said he will discuss the final date in Moscow on Monday.

"We're shooting for next week, but I can't be any more specific than that because we'll probably be meeting on Monday with the medical team and making that decision," DeBakey told thje British Broadcasting Corporation.
DeBakey said doctors were expecting three or four bypasses. The Russian team will be led by cardiologist Renat Akchurin, who will use equipment from DeBakey's Houston centre.
DeBakey said Yeltsin should be able to resume normal duties within six weeks to two months if the operation succeeds. "He should be able to have another 10 years of good work life."
Yeltsin's absence from office, already four months, has caused much speculation about his chances of returning to work and has prompted fierce fights, mostly backstage, among top Kremlin officials.
On Wednesday the communist head of the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, demanded the sacking of the Yeltsin's chief-of-staff.

The Duma chairman Gennady Seleznyov said he was not happy with the appointment of businessman Boris Berezovsky as deputy secretary of Yeltsin's Security Council -- an advisory board comprising top officials.

Seleznyov accused the chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais of engineering Berzovsky's nomination and said he would not take part in a newly established consultative council on which Chubais is also due to sit.

Yeltsin had hoped the four-member council, which also includes Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Yegor Stroyev, head of the upper chamber of parliament, would help avert the in-fighting that has plagued recent Russian politics.
Chubais, brought into the Kremlin in July, is a hate figure for Russia's communists, who despise his privatisation programme and the free-market economic reforms he helped to launch.

In another upset to Yeltsin's team some influential regional leaders made clear on Wednesday they were not happy with the Kremlin's latest efforts to consolidate control over 89 regions which form the Russian Federation.
Chubais blamed the regional leadership for encouraging legislation which violated the Federation's constitution.
He said the Kremlin would take tough measures to ensure that nothing is done in Russia which would undermine Moscow's interests.
Interfax news agency quoted the head of the ethnic republic of North Ossetia, Akhsarbek Galazov, as warning the Kremlin that attacks on regional powers could turn against Moscow itself.
"Any humiliation of regional power will help Russia's enemies," added Galazov, generally known for his pro-Moscow views. "Then a threat of separatism could emerge."
